---
title: "What Is Fair Learning?"
---



Start with a sign-off that every model-risk team has seen.

> *"The model is fair.  It doesn't even use the protected attribute."*

Then an audit shows its scores still track that attribute — cleanly enough
to reconstruct it.  Nobody lied: the attribute really was deleted from the
inputs, and the standard correlation check really did come back near zero.
**The number said neutral.  The dependence was there.**  This chapter is
about closing the distance between those two sentences — and the tools are
exactly the dependence measures of
[the dependence chapter](../dependence/index.qmd), now pointed at a model's
own output.

## What Counts as Unfair?

A model is **unfair** when its decision would change if we flipped only a
**protected attribute** $S$ — sex, race, age — and held everything else
fixed.  Credit, hiring, bail, insurance: the score should track *risk*, not
*who you are*.  Stated as a property of the prediction $\hat y$, the goal is

$$
\hat y \;\perp\; S
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\operatorname{Dep}(\hat y, S) = 0 ,
$$

independence between the score and the attribute — the criterion known as
**statistical parity**.  The left side is a moral requirement; the right
side is a *measurable quantity*.  That equivalence is the whole chapter:
once "fair" is a dependence, it can be audited with a number and trained
against with a penalty.

*(Other fairness criteria — equalized odds, sufficiency — condition on the
true outcome $y$ before demanding independence.  They are different and
sometimes mutually incompatible choices, but every one of them is a
dependence statement; we work with independence because it maps directly
onto the tools we have.)*

## The Three Layers

Where does the unfairness physically live?  Three layers, two arrows:

::: {#cell-fig-three-layers .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch, FancyArrowPatch

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.5, 3.4))
ax.set_xlim(0, 10); ax.set_ylim(0, 4.8); ax.axis("off")
boxes = [(1.7, "S", "sensitive\n(sex, race, age)", CRASH),
         (5.0, "X", "features / data\n(carry proxies for S)", COOL),
         (8.3, "ŷ", "prediction\n(the decision)", GREEN)]
for x0, sym, sub, col in boxes:
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x0 - 0.9, 1.5), 1.8, 1.0,
                                boxstyle="round,pad=0.08",
                                fc="white", ec=col, lw=2.6))
    ax.text(x0, 2.0, sym, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=21, color=col,
            fontweight="bold")
    ax.text(x0, 0.85, sub, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10, color=INK)
for (x0, x1, lbl) in [(2.7, 4.0, "leaks"), (6.0, 7.3, "model")]:
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x0, 2.0), (x1, 2.0), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                 mutation_scale=18, lw=2, color=INK))
    ax.text((x0 + x1) / 2, 2.28, lbl, ha="center", fontsize=10, color=INK)
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((8.3, 2.55), (1.7, 2.55),
                             connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.30",
                             arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=18, lw=2,
                             ls="--", color=WARM))
ax.text(5.0, 4.55, "fairness audit:  is  ŷ  independent of  S ?",
        ha="center", fontsize=13, color=WARM, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![The anatomy of an unfair model. The sensitive attribute S leaks into the features X (zip code, occupation, sector); the model faithfully passes whatever is in X through to the prediction ŷ. The audit — and the training penalty — both attack the dashed link: is ŷ independent of S?](01-what-is-fair_files/figure-html/fig-three-layers-output-1.png){#fig-three-layers width=1000 height=339}
:::
:::


The bias hides in the *arrows*, not the boxes.  $S$ **leaks** into the
features — through zip code, occupation, hours worked, sector membership —
and the model, doing exactly its job, passes whatever predictive signal is
in $X$ through to $\hat y$.  Deleting the $S$ column removes a box, not the
arrows.  The audit (and later the training penalty) targets the dashed
link directly: measure $\operatorname{Dep}(\hat y, S)$, and drive it down.

## The Itch — The Standard Check Is Blind

So we need a number for the dashed link.  The standard sign-off uses the
cheapest one — Pearson correlation between score and attribute — and that
choice is exactly where the opening story goes wrong.  Correlation sees
straight lines; a score can bend with $S$ and still correlate at zero.
This is the fairness mirror of the dependence chapter's
[bad morning](../dependence/01-correlation.qmd): the number said safe, the
dependence was there.

::: {#cell-fig-fair-hook .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n = 700
S = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
score = (S**2 - 1) + 0.4 * rng.normal(0, 1, n)  # depends on S — but curvily

pear = pearsonr(score, S)[0]
ck = cka_rbf(score, S)

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2))

axL.scatter(S, score, s=12, c=COOL, alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")
axL.set_title("The standard check", fontsize=12)
annotate_box(axL, 0.5, -0.10, f"Pearson(score, S) = {pear:+.2f}   ← looks neutral")
despine(axL)

bins = np.linspace(S.min(), S.max(), 11)
idx = np.digitize(S, bins)
centers = 0.5 * (bins[:-1] + bins[1:])
means = [score[idx == k].mean() for k in range(1, len(bins))]
axR.scatter(S, score, s=10, c=COOL, alpha=0.18, edgecolors="none")
axR.plot(centers, means, "-o", c=CRASH, lw=2.2, label="mean score per bin")
axR.set_title("The honest audit", fontsize=12)
annotate_box(axR, 0.5, -0.10, f"CKA(score, S) = {ck:.2f}   ← strongly dependent")
axR.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False)
despine(axR)

for ax in (axL, axR):
    ax.set_xlabel("sensitive variable S"); ax.set_ylabel("model score")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Left: the standard check — Pearson ≈ 0 against S, sign-off granted. Right: bin S and plot the mean score per bin — the score bends with S all along, and CKA (the kernel measure from the dependence chapter) reports the dependence the correlation missed.](01-what-is-fair_files/figure-html/fig-fair-hook-output-1.png){#fig-fair-hook width=1304 height=489}
:::
:::


The fix is not a better lawyer — it is a better measure.  Every audit in
this chapter will use one that sees curves
([CKA](../dependence/02-kernels-hsic.qmd), the normalized HSIC), and every
training method will be graded against it.

## The Objective — The Whole Chapter in One Line

Perfect neutrality usually costs accuracy, so we do not demand it — we
**price** it:

$$
\text{loss} \;=\;
\underbrace{\text{fit}(\hat y, y)}_{\text{predict well}}
\;+\; \mu \cdot
\underbrace{\operatorname{Dep}(\hat y, S)}_{\text{stay blind to } S} .
$$

`fit` is your usual prediction error.  $\operatorname{Dep}$ is any
dependence measure from [the dependence chapter](../dependence/index.qmd),
applied between the *predictions* and $S$.  The weight $\mu$ trades accuracy
against neutrality.  The [ladder of removal](03-fair-kernel-learning.qmd)
is just a sequence of choices for $\operatorname{Dep}$, from cheap-and-blind
to flexible-and-expensive — and this objective is, structurally, the same
move as the uncertainty chapter's
[regression recipe](../uncertainty/04-regression-recipe.qmd): change what
you want from the model by changing the *loss*, then let the optimizer do
the negotiating.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Background — The Penalty Is a Lagrangian

What we actually want is a *constrained* problem: minimize prediction error
subject to "no dependence on $S$,"

$$
\min_{\theta}\; \mathbb{E}\,[\,\ell(\hat y_\theta, y)\,]
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \operatorname{Dep}(\hat y_\theta, S) = 0.
$$

Forming the Lagrangian turns the constraint into the additive penalty we
train with,

$$
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\,[\,\ell(\hat y_\theta, y)\,]
+ \mu\,\operatorname{Dep}(\hat y_\theta, S),
$$

where $\mu$ is the Lagrange multiplier.  Sweeping $\mu$ from $0$ to
$\infty$ traces the **Pareto frontier** between accuracy and neutrality —
exactly the [trade-off curve](03-fair-kernel-learning.qmd) this chapter
builds to.  There is no single "fair model"; there is a curve, and $\mu$
chooses your operating point.
:::

## Two Framings, One Operation

The same objective wears two names in finance:

- **Fairness.** $S$ is a protected attribute (sex, race, age).  Regulation —
  the EU's [GDPR](https://gdpr.eu/) Art. 22 on automated decisions, and the
  **EU AI Act**, which classes credit scoring and CV screening as
  *high-risk* — requires that decisions not depend on such attributes.  A
  credit model must approve on ability to repay, not on group membership.
- **Factor-neutrality.** $S$ is a market or sector factor (beta).  A
  strategy that must be *market-neutral* should produce returns that don't
  load on the factor it is hedging.

"Don't discriminate" and "don't load on the factor I'm hedging" are the
same maths: drive $\operatorname{Dep}(\hat y, S)$ to zero.  The
[credit lab](labs/lab-jobB-neutralize-credit.qmd) and the
[beta-neutral lab](labs/lab-jobC-beta-neutral.qmd) run the *identical code*
on both problems.

::: {.eli5}
**One-liner.**  Fair learning doesn't *hide* the sensitive variable — it adds
"depend on $S$" to the bill, so the optimizer chooses to stop using it.
:::

Next: why the obvious fix — just delete $S$ —
[doesn't work](02-bias-and-proxies.qmd).
